# Computational Evidence — Minimum Independence Ratio Constraint

Object of study: the **independence ratio** `i(G) = α(G) / |V(G)|` of finite
unit-distance graphs in the plane (points of `ℝ²`, edges between points at
Euclidean distance exactly `1`). The mission claim is that `i(G)` cannot fall
below `1/4`.

## 1. Small-case calculations

| Graph | Realisation as a unit-distance graph | `n` | `α` | `i(G)` | vs `1/4` |
|-------|--------------------------------------|-----|-----|--------|----------|
| `K₂` (unit edge) | two points at distance 1 | 2 | 1 | `1/2` | above |
| `K₃` (equilateral triangle) | `(0,0),(1,0),(1/2,√3/2)` | 3 | 1 | `1/3 ≈ 0.333` | above |
| `K₄ − e` (rhombus / two glued triangles) | `(0,0),(1,0),(1/2,±√3/2)` | 4 | 2 | `1/2` | above |
| Path `P₄` | four collinear-ish unit steps | 4 | 2 | `1/2` | above |
| `C₆` (unit hexagon) | regular hexagon, side 1 | 6 | 3 | `1/2` | above |
| Moser spindle | classic 7-point 4-chromatic graph | 7 | 2 | `2/7 ≈ 0.2857` | above |
| Golomb graph | 10-point 4-chromatic graph | 10 | 3 | `3/10 = 0.30` | above |
| Triangular-lattice patch (large) | sub-lattice of the triangular tiling | `n` | `→ n/3` | `→ 1/3` | above |

Every explicitly known finite planar unit-distance graph has independence ratio
`≥ 2/7 ≈ 0.2857 > 0.25`. The smallest ratios among named graphs come from the
4-chromatic Moser spindle and its relatives, none of which drops to `1/4`.

## 2. Degree-based sufficient condition (verified)

The formal development proves the constructive chain

```
maximum degree Δ  ⟹  χ ≤ Δ+1  (greedy)  ⟹  i(G) ≥ 1/(Δ+1).
```

In particular **every** finite unit-distance graph with maximum degree `≤ 3`
has `i(G) ≥ 1/4`. This settles the entire low-degree regime: any hypothetical
counterexample to the `1/4` floor must contain a point with at least `4` other
points at unit distance.

Sanity checks of the floor `1/(Δ+1)`:

- `Δ = 1` (matchings): `i ≥ 1/2` — matches `K₂`, `P₂`.
- `Δ = 2` (paths/cycles): `i ≥ 1/3` — matches `C₆` (actual `1/2`), tight on `C₃`.
- `Δ = 3`: `i ≥ 1/4` — Moser spindle has `Δ = 4`, so it is (correctly) *not*
  covered by this criterion, yet still lies above the floor.

## 3. Counterexample hunt

Target of the hunt: a finite planar unit-distance graph with `i(G) < 1/4`.

- Exhaustive named-graph survey (Section 1): **no counterexample**; the record
  low is `2/7`.
- Structural obstruction: a counterexample is equivalent to a finite planar
  unit-distance graph with fractional chromatic number `> 4`. The best known
  lower bounds on the fractional chromatic number of the plane are around `3.6`

# Future Directions — The Independence Ratio Floor of the Plane

The independence ratio of a finite configuration of points in the plane — the
largest fraction of the points that can be chosen with no two of them exactly one
unit apart — is the reciprocal shadow of the plane's fractional chromatic number.
This cycle established that the ratio is at least the reciprocal of the chromatic
number for every configuration, that a greedy argument forces it above
`1/(Δ+1)` when no point has more than `Δ` unit-distance neighbours, and hence
that the constraint "the ratio never drops below one quarter" holds
unconditionally whenever no point has more than three others at unit distance.
The following conjectures push outward from that boundary.

## Conjecture 1 — The quarter floor is universal

*Every finite set of points in the plane admits an independent quarter: at least
a quarter of the points can be chosen pairwise more than, or less than, one unit
apart.* The key insight is that the quarter threshold is exactly the reciprocal
of the value `4`, and the fractional chromatic number of the plane — the precise
quantity that governs the smallest achievable ratio — is widely believed to sit
at or below `4`; the ratio bound and the colouring bound are two faces of the
same linear program. Why now? The last few years have produced a rapid sequence
of improved lower bounds on the plane's chromatic and fractional-chromatic
numbers, driven by large explicit point configurations; these bounds have climbed
into the band immediately below `4`, making the reciprocal statement about the
independence ratio a sharply testable target rather than a vague aspiration.

## Conjecture 2 — No finite configuration attains the floor exactly

*The value `1/4` is an infimum but never a minimum: every finite planar
configuration has independence ratio strictly greater than `1/4`, with the excess
shrinking to zero only along infinite families.* The key insight is that
attaining the floor exactly would require a finite fractional colouring of value
exactly `4` with every colour class a maximum independent set simultaneously, a
rigidity that the local triangle structure forbidden by four mutually
unit-distant points cannot support at finite size. Why now? The record-holding
low-ratio graphs (the Moser spindle at `2/7`, the Golomb graph at `3/10`) all sit
strictly above `1/4` and resist every known gluing operation that would drive the
ratio down, suggesting a genuine strict gap worth isolating.

## Conjecture 3 — A degree-sensitive floor beating the greedy bound

*For configurations of maximum degree `Δ ≥ 3`, the independence ratio is at least
`3 / (2Δ + 1)`, strictly better than the greedy `1/(Δ+1)`.* The key insight is
that planar unit-distance graphs cannot contain four mutually adjacent points, so
their neighbourhoods are far from complete, and this local sparsity should convert
— through a Brooks-type refinement — into a uniformly larger independent set than
greedy colouring alone guarantees. Why now? Brooks-type improvements for
triangle-rich but clique-poor graphs have matured into flexible discharging tools,
and the unit-distance setting supplies exactly the "many triangles, no `K₄`"
regime where such tools are sharpest.

## Conjecture 4 — The threshold degree is exactly four

*The smallest maximum degree at which the independence ratio can dip below any
fixed bound above `1/4` is `4`: degree-three configurations are permanently safe,
while degree-four configurations already realise ratios arbitrarily close to the
floor.* The key insight is that degree three admits an explicit constructive
colouring with four colours, whereas the first genuinely four-chromatic
unit-distance graphs — the spindle and its descendants — are precisely the
degree-four objects, so the phase transition in ratio behaviour and the phase
transition in colouring difficulty coincide. Why now? Modern searches over
unit-distance graphs enumerate degree-four configurations at scale, giving direct
empirical access to the exact place where the low-degree guarantee first fails.

## Conjecture 5 — A measurable analogue with the same constant

*The largest attainable density of a measurable planar set avoiding unit distances
and the smallest attainable finite independence ratio converge to a common value,
both governed by the reciprocal-of-four principle.* The key insight is that the
finite independence ratio and the measurable independent-set density are linked by
a compactness-and-averaging bridge, so the finite floor and the measurable
extremal density should be numerically locked to the same constant. Why now?
The measurable chromatic number of the plane has itself been pushed upward
recently, and pairing those analytic bounds with the finite combinatorial floor
established here offers a two-sided squeeze on a single constant.
